questions.prompt: What does `console.log(a); var a = 1;` print?
questions.explanation: The `var` declaration is hoisted and set to `undefined`; the assignment stays on its line.

questions.prompt: What does `console.log(b); let b = 1;` do?
questions.explanation: `let` is hoisted but not initialised. Until its line runs, it is in the temporal dead zone.

questions.prompt: What does `hello(); function hello() { console.log("hi"); }` print?

questions.prompt: What does `console.log(typeof x); var x = () => 1;` print?

questions.prompt: What does `var x = 1; function f() { console.log(x); var x = 2; } f();` print?
questions.explanation: The inner `var x` is hoisted to the top of `f` and hides the outer `x`, but it has no value yet.

questions.prompt: What does `console.log(typeof notDeclared);` print, when `notDeclared` is never declared anywhere?
questions.explanation: `typeof` is safe on undeclared names. Reading the name in any other way would throw.

questions.prompt: What does `let x = 1; { console.log(x); let x = 2; }` do?
questions.explanation: The inner `let x` is hoisted to the top of the block, so the outer `x` is hidden and the inner one is still in its dead zone.

questions.prompt: What does `function f() { return g(); function g() { return 1; } } console.log(f());` print?
questions.explanation: `g` is a declaration, so it is hoisted inside `f` and exists before the `return` runs.

questions.prompt: What does `var f = 1; function f() {} console.log(typeof f);` print?
questions.explanation: The function declaration is hoisted first, then the line `f = 1` runs and replaces it.
`x` exists from the start with `undefined`, and gets 5 when its line runs.
The local `var name` is hoisted inside `show`, so the first log sees it before it has a value.
`a` is in its dead zone. `b` is a hoisted `var` without its value yet. `c` is a hoisted function declaration.

questions.prompt: What does `console.log(a); var a = 1;` print, and why?
key_points: It prints `undefined`
The declaration is hoisted, but the assignment stays on its line
`var` variables start with the value `undefined` at the top of their scope
questions.correct_answer: It prints `undefined`. Before the code runs, JavaScript sets up every `var` in the scope and gives it the value `undefined`. The assignment `a = 1` only happens when its line runs, so at the `console.log`, `a` exists but has no value yet.

questions.prompt: What happens with the same code using `let`, and why?
key_points: It throws a ReferenceError
`let` is hoisted but not initialised
From the start of the block until its line, the variable is in the temporal dead zone
This makes the bug visible instead of quietly giving `undefined`
questions.correct_answer: With `let`, `console.log(a)` throws a ReferenceError. `let` is also hoisted, so JavaScript knows the name, but it is not given any value until its line runs. The time between the start of the block and the declaration is the temporal dead zone, and using the variable there throws. This is better than `var`, because the mistake shows up straight away.

questions.prompt: What is hoisted for `var`, `let`, `const`, function declarations and function expressions?
key_points: `var` is hoisted and set to `undefined`
`let` and `const` are hoisted but stay in the temporal dead zone until their line
Function declarations are hoisted with their whole body
Function expressions and arrow functions follow the rule of the variable that holds them
Class declarations behave like `let`
questions.correct_answer: `var` is hoisted and starts as `undefined`. `let` and `const` are hoisted too, but using them before their line throws, because of the temporal dead zone. Function declarations are hoisted completely, so you can call them anywhere in their scope. A function expression or arrow function is just a value in a variable, so it follows that variable's rule: `undefined` with `var`, an error with `let` or `const`. Classes act like `let`.

questions.prompt: What does `for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i));` print?
questions.explanation: `let` gives each iteration its own `i`.

questions.prompt: What does `for (var i = 0; i < 2; i++) {} console.log(i);` print?
questions.explanation: `var` is not block scoped, so `i` still exists after the loop, holding the value that ended it.

questions.prompt: What does `for (let i = 0; i < 2; i++) {} console.log(i);` do?
questions.explanation: With `let`, `i` exists only inside the loop.

questions.prompt: What does `for (var i = 1; i <= 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i), i * 10);` print?
questions.explanation: The delays use the value at the time, but the callbacks read the shared `i` later, after the loop pushed it to 4.

questions.prompt: What does `const fns = []; for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) fns.push(() => i * 2); console.log(fns[2]());` print?
questions.explanation: The third function has its own `i`, which is 2.

questions.prompt: What does `var fns = []; for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) fns.push(() => i * 2); console.log(fns[0]());` print?
questions.explanation: All the functions share one `i`, which is 3 after the loop, so 3 * 2.

questions.prompt: What does `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(((j) => () => console.log(j))(i));` print?
questions.explanation: The outer arrow runs immediately with the current `i` as `j`, and returns a callback that keeps its own `j`.

questions.prompt: What does `let i = 0; for (; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i));` print?
questions.explanation: `i` is declared outside the loop, so there is only one `i`, even though it is a `let`.

questions.prompt: What does `for (const x of [1, 2, 3]) setTimeout(() => console.log(x));` print?
questions.explanation: `for...of` creates a new `x` for each value, so `const` is fine and each callback keeps its own.
One shared `i`, read after the loop has finished.
The label is built right away, but the click handler reads `i` later, when it is 3.

questions.correct_answer: sync 3 var 3 var 3 var 3 let 0 let 1 let 2
questions.explanation: The sync log runs first. The `var` timers share one `i`; the `let` timers each have their own `j`.

questions.prompt: What does `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i));` print, and why?
key_points: It prints `3 3 3`
There is one `i` shared by the whole loop
The callbacks run after the loop has finished, when `i` is 3
questions.correct_answer: It prints `3 3 3`. Because of `var`, the whole loop has a single `i`. The `setTimeout` callbacks do not run during the loop; they run after it has finished, and by then `i` has reached 3. All three callbacks read that same variable.

questions.prompt: What changes if you use `let`, and why?
key_points: It prints `0 1 2`
`let` creates a new `i` for each iteration
Each callback closes over its own `i`
questions.correct_answer: With `let` it prints `0 1 2`. A `let` in a `for` loop gets a fresh copy for each iteration, starting from the previous value. Each callback closes over the copy from its own iteration, so each prints a different number.

questions.prompt: Click handlers created in a `var` loop all use the last index. Explain why and give two fixes.
key_points: The handlers close over one shared `var` variable and run later, when clicked
By then the variable holds its final value
Fix 1: use `let`, which gives each iteration its own variable
Fix 2: use `forEach`, an IIFE, or pass the index as an argument or a data attribute
questions.correct_answer: Each handler is a closure over the same `var i`, and it only runs when someone clicks, long after the loop has finished. By then `i` holds its final value, so every handler uses it. The simplest fix is to use `let`, so each iteration has its own `i`. Another is to loop with `forEach((item, index) => ...)`, where each call has its own `index`, or to store the index in a `data-` attribute and read it in one delegated handler.

questions.prompt: What does `console.log(1); setTimeout(() => console.log(2)); console.log(3);` print?
questions.explanation: The timer callback waits until the synchronous code has finished.

questions.prompt: What does `Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("a")); console.log("b");` print?
questions.explanation: Even an already resolved promise runs its `.then` callback later, as a microtask.

questions.prompt: What does `setTimeout(() => console.log("t")); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("p"));` print?
questions.explanation: Microtasks run before the next macrotask, even though the timer was set first.

questions.prompt: What does `new Promise((r) => { console.log(1); r(); }).then(() => console.log(2)); console.log(3);` print?
questions.explanation: The executor runs synchronously. Only the `.then` callback waits.

questions.prompt: What does `setTimeout(() => console.log(1), 10); setTimeout(() => console.log(2), 0);` print?
questions.explanation: Timers run when they are due, so the 0 ms one runs first.

questions.prompt: What does `(async () => { console.log(1); await null; console.log(2); })(); console.log(3);` print?
questions.explanation: The async function runs until the `await`; the rest continues as a microtask after the sync code.

questions.prompt: What does `setTimeout(() => { console.log(1); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(2)); }); setTimeout(() => console.log(3));` print?
questions.explanation: After the first timer task, its microtask runs before the event loop takes the second timer.

questions.prompt: What does `Promise.resolve().then(() => { console.log(1); setTimeout(() => console.log(2)); }); setTimeout(() => console.log(3));` print?
questions.explanation: The microtask runs first and schedules a new timer, which goes behind the timer that was already queued.

questions.prompt: What does `Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(1)).then(() => console.log(2)); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(3));` print?
questions.explanation: The second `.then` of the first chain is only queued once 1 has run, so 3 is already ahead of it.
Sync code, then microtasks, then macrotasks.

questions.correct_answer: async start sync async end then timeout
questions.explanation: The code after `await` was queued before the `.then`, so it runs first. Both run before the timer.

questions.correct_answer: A G D F B C E
questions.explanation: Sync first (A, G), then all microtasks (D, F). Then timer B runs, followed by its microtask C, and finally timer E.

questions.prompt: What does `console.log(1); setTimeout(() => console.log(2)); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(3)); console.log(4);` print, and why?
key_points: It prints `1 4 3 2`
Synchronous code runs first, so 1 and 4
Promise callbacks are microtasks and run before timers, which are macrotasks
questions.correct_answer: It prints `1 4 3 2`. The two plain `console.log` calls are synchronous, so 1 and 4 print first. Then the event loop runs the microtask queue, which holds the promise callback, so 3 prints. Only after that does it take the timer callback from the task queue, so 2 prints last.

questions.prompt: How do you work out the print order of a snippet that mixes sync code, promises and timers?
key_points: Run all the synchronous code first, including promise executors and async code before its first `await`
Then run the microtasks in the order they were queued, including any new ones added along the way
Then run one macrotask, then its microtasks, and repeat
Timers are ordered by delay, then by the order they were set
questions.correct_answer: First go through the synchronous code line by line, remembering that promise executors and the start of async functions, up to the first `await`, are synchronous too. Then empty the microtask queue in order: `.then` callbacks and code after `await`, including any microtasks added while doing this. Then take one macrotask, like the earliest due timer, run it, and empty the microtasks again. Repeat until nothing is left.

questions.prompt: Why does code after `await` run before a `setTimeout(fn, 0)` that was set earlier?
key_points: The code after `await` continues as a microtask
The `setTimeout` callback is a macrotask
The event loop empties the microtask queue before it takes the next macrotask
So even a timer set earlier has to wait
questions.correct_answer: When an async function hits `await`, the rest of the function is scheduled to continue as a microtask once the promise settles. The `setTimeout` callback, even with 0 ms, goes into the macrotask queue. The event loop always finishes every microtask before taking the next macrotask, so the code after `await` runs first, even if the timer was created earlier.

questions.prompt: What does `const greet = user.greet; greet();` return, where `greet` returns `this.name`? Why?
key_points: It does not return the user's name
In strict mode `this` is `undefined`, so it throws; otherwise `this` is the global object
`this` is decided by how the function is called, and a plain call has no object
questions.correct_answer: It does not return the user's name. `greet` is now called as a plain function, with no object before the dot, so `this` is not `user`. In strict mode, including classes and modules, `this` is `undefined` and reading `this.name` throws a TypeError. In sloppy mode, `this` is the global object, which usually has no `name`.

questions.prompt: Give three ways to keep `this` when passing a method as a callback.
key_points: `bind`: pass `obj.method.bind(obj)`
Wrap it in an arrow function: `() => obj.method()`
Define the method as an arrow function class field
Explains that each keeps the object as `this` when the callback runs
questions.correct_answer: First, `obj.method.bind(obj)` creates a function whose `this` is locked to `obj`. Second, you can pass `() => obj.method()`, so the method is still called on the object. Third, in a class you can write the method as an arrow function field, `handleClick = () => { ... }`, so each instance has its own copy that always uses that instance as `this`.

questions.prompt: Why do class methods lose `this` in React event handlers, and how did class components fix it?
key_points: `onClick={this.handleClick}` passes the function without its object
React calls it as a plain function, and class code is strict, so `this` is `undefined`
The classic fix is binding in the constructor: `this.handleClick = this.handleClick.bind(this)`
Arrow function class fields also fix it
Function components with hooks avoid `this` entirely
questions.correct_answer: Writing `onClick={this.handleClick}` hands React just the function. When React calls it later, it is a plain call, and because class code is strict, `this` is `undefined`, so `this.setState` throws. Class components fixed this by binding in the constructor, `this.handleClick = this.handleClick.bind(this)`, or by writing handlers as arrow function class fields. Modern function components with hooks do not use `this` at all, so the problem disappears.

questions.prompt: What does `[] + []` give?
questions.explanation: Each empty array becomes an empty string, and two empty strings joined give an empty string.

questions.prompt: What does `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` give?
questions.explanation: `0.1 + 0.2` is actually `0.30000000000000004`, because of how decimals are stored.

questions.prompt: What does `"5" * 2` give?
questions.explanation: `*` only works on numbers, so "5" is turned into 5. Only `+` prefers strings.

questions.prompt: What does `[] + {}` give?
questions.explanation: `[]` becomes "" and `{}` becomes "[object Object]", then they are joined.

questions.prompt: What does `[1, 2] + [3]` give?
questions.explanation: Arrays become strings with commas: "1,2" and "3", then `+` joins them.

questions.prompt: How should you check whether `0.1 + 0.2` equals `0.3`?
questions.explanation: Compare with a small tolerance. For money, store whole cents instead.

questions.prompt: What does `NaN === NaN` give, and how do you test for `NaN`?
questions.explanation: `NaN` is the only value not equal to itself. The global `isNaN("abc")` is true, because it converts to a number first.

questions.prompt: What does `[10, 1, 2].sort()` give?
questions.explanation: Without a compare function, `sort` compares values as strings. Use `sort((a, b) => a - b)`.

questions.prompt: What does `0.1 * 3` give?
questions.explanation: 0.1 cannot be stored exactly in binary, and the small error shows up after the multiplication.

questions.prompt: console.log("5" + 1, "5" - 1);
questions.explanation: With a string, `+` joins text. `-` only works on numbers, so "5" becomes 5.

questions.prompt: console.log(JSON.stringify([] + []), [] + {}, [1] == 1);
questions.explanation: `[] + []` is an empty string, shown with quotes by `JSON.stringify`. `[1]` becomes "1", then 1, so `==` is true.
The sum has a tiny rounding error, but `toFixed` rounds it. `sort` compares as strings. "abc" * 1 is `NaN`.

key_points: Numbers are stored as binary floating point (IEEE 754)
0.1 and 0.2 cannot be stored exactly, so they have tiny rounding errors
Compare with a small tolerance or round; store money as whole cents
questions.correct_answer: JavaScript stores numbers in binary floating point. Just as 1/3 has no exact decimal form, 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary form, so each is stored with a tiny error. Added together, the result is `0.30000000000000004`, which is not exactly 0.3. Compare with a small tolerance like `Number.EPSILON`, round for display, and keep money in whole cents.

questions.prompt: What do `[] + []` and `[] + {}` give, and why?
key_points: `+` with an object first converts both sides to primitives
An array becomes a string with `toString`, so `[]` becomes `""`
`{}` becomes `"[object Object]"`
Then `+` joins strings, giving `""` and `"[object Object]"`
questions.correct_answer: When `+` sees an object, it first turns both sides into primitives. Arrays turn into strings by joining their items with commas, so an empty array becomes an empty string. A plain object becomes "[object Object]". Since at least one side is now a string, `+` joins strings: `[] + []` is "", and `[] + {}` is "[object Object]".

questions.prompt: How do you avoid coercion bugs in real code?
key_points: Use `===` and `!==` instead of `==`
Convert values on purpose with `Number()` or `String()`, for example form inputs
Check for `NaN` with `Number.isNaN`
Sort numbers with a compare function like `(a, b) => a - b`
Keep money in whole cents, and use TypeScript to catch type mix-ups
questions.correct_answer: Always compare with `===` so JavaScript does not convert types behind your back. Convert values yourself, for example `Number(input.value)`, since form fields are always strings. Check for `NaN` with `Number.isNaN`, and sort numbers with `(a, b) => a - b`. Store money in whole cents to avoid floating point errors. TypeScript also helps, because it flags places where a string is used as a number.
